body.heading: How air fills with droplets
paragraphs: Fog is a cloud of tiny water droplets suspended in air near the surface, dense enough to cut visibility below one kilometre. It forms when air cools to its dew point — often on clear, calm nights, when the ground radiates heat away and chills the air resting on it — or when warm, moist air drifts over a cold surface, as happens along chilly coasts.

Each droplet needs a speck to form on, and city air, rich in particles, grows thick fogs readily. A single cubic metre of fog may hold hundreds of millions of droplets, yet all of them together amount to barely a sip of water.

body.heading: Beautiful and hazardous
paragraphs: Fog muffles sound, softens outlines and can turn a familiar street into a strange, quiet world within minutes. It also arrives with real dangers: it is among the deadliest weather conditions for drivers, because visibility can collapse faster than speed can adjust.

For some ecosystems, fog is a lifeline. Coastal redwoods harvest a significant share of their water from fog dripping off their needles, and desert beetles in Namibia collect fog droplets on their backs and drink. One place's hazard is another's water supply.

takeaway: Fog is simply a cloud at ground level, forming when air cools to saturation and water condenses into tiny droplets.
